newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO rebuffs Russia over Baltic states.
newsitem.headline: NATO rebuffs Russia over Baltic states.

text.p: NATO rebuffed Russian resistance to the Baltic states joining the Western defence group on Tuesday, highlighting a rift between the alliance and Moscow despite their new partnership deal.

"It is absolutely clear that the Baltic states continue to be eligible for NATO membership," alliance spokesman Jamie Shea told a news conference at a Russia-NATO summit in Paris where the former Cold War foes signed the partnership accord.
"We do not see them as former Soviet Union countries with some special category as a result of the past."

Russia and the West appear to be drawing battle lines for a new round of tough talks on NATO expansion after the first wave begins in July, when the alliance is due to offer membership to some eastern European countries.

President Boris Yeltsin criticised NATO's plans to take in Moscow's former Soviet-bloc allies just before signing the deal on Tuesday but has been forced to acknowledge that a first wave of expansion will go ahead.

Russian officials are now anxious to prevent former Soviet republics being included in any later waves of expansion, saying this is an unacceptable security theat which would bring NATO right up to Russia's borders.

They have singled out for special mention the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which were annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940 and now want to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
"If NATO tries to take in the former Soviet republics, we will have to reconsider our whole relationship with the West," a senior Russian delegation member told Reuters in Paris.
Russian officials say they believe the West understands their concerns and will not seek a new battle.
But Shea stuck to basic principles. "NATO will not do anything which puts the Baltic states into a separate category and consigns them to a different security sphere," he said.
He said many countries had been swallowed by other countries during their history and added: "That does not mean that they have to suffer any restraint in their sovereignty or freedom of action."

Russia is still a dominant force in many parts of the former Soviet Union because the former republics have struggled financially since the Union collapsed in 1991 and have traditional trade and political ties with Moscow.

Russia wants to increase integration with these countries and is keen to prevent itself being totally cut off from the enclave of Kaliningrad by NATO countries. This would happen if Lithuania and Poland join the alliance.
The presidents of Poland, Ukraine and the Baltic states met at a special regional summit on Tuesday and hailed the pact between NATO and Russia as a boost to European security and stability.

"The presidents expressed their satisfaction with the signing on the same day in Paris of the Founding Act on bilateral cooperation and security between NATO and Russia," the leaders said in a joint statement.
"In their view, the Founding Act enhances mutual confidence, security and stability in the Euro-Atlantic area," they said.
The Estonian hosts of the meeting said it was not a demonstration of solidarity against Russia.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are all expected to be invited to join the alliance at a July summit in Madrid.
Ukraine does not wish to join the alliance but wants a special cooperation treaty with NATO.
